turns.content: We are comparing ways cells regulate multicellular development: localized mRNA trafficking; protein phosphorylation and ubiquitination; DNA methylation, histone acetylation, and small RNAs; and short sugar molecules used to sense neighboring cells and coordinate population density. What biological criteria would help identify the least characteristic mechanism?
How can phosphorylation and ubiquitination change protein activity or abundance, and why might those changes matter during development?
Compare epigenetic and small-RNA regulation with the short-sugar neighbor-sensing proposal. Which established biological processes does each description resemble?
Which of these mechanisms is least characteristic of regulation in multicellular development? Explain the distinction in biological terms.
Consider localized mRNA trafficking more closely. How can moving an mRNA change where its protein is produced without changing the DNA sequence?
Using that mechanism, assess whether localized mRNA trafficking is a plausible form of developmental regulation under the same broad organismal scope.
State the least characteristic mechanism and calibrate your confidence. How do the broad organismal scope and the imprecise description of short-sugar signaling limit the conclusion?

Check the comparison against the established roles of RNA localization, protein modification, and epigenetic regulation. Does the conclusion depend on treating any of these mechanisms as universally absent?
Give your final assessment with a concise mechanistic rationale and the qualifications needed for this broad comparison.
